facts.claim: The Billy Strings EP's liner notes credit the recording of 'Dust in a Baggie' to April 11–12, 2016 at Minutia Studios in Nashville. Shalini Gandhi was the recording and mixing engineer, and Anna Frick mastered it at Airshow Studios in Boulder, CO.

The EP credits Billy Strings on guitar, lead vocal and banjo, Casey Campbell on mandolin, John Mailander on fiddle, Billy Failing on banjo and backing vocal, and Erik Alvar on upright bass. The song is credited to William Apostol (Billy Strings).
Billy Strings released the self-titled, six-song EP on June 10, 2016. 'Dust in a Baggie' is its closing track.
The song first appeared on record on the 2013 album 'Rock of Ages', a collaboration with mandolinist Don Julin. The 2016 EP version is a re-recording.
Strings said he wrote the song in about 30 minutes at work, with no guitar, just a melody in his head and a little notepad.
Strings told Theo Von the song is about Brad Lasco. He said the 'Me/And/Dad' record was dedicated to Lasco, who had died a couple of years earlier.
Strings said the song is about a man who ruined his life and sits in prison wondering where he went wrong. He added that some traditional bluegrass fans dismissed it as a song about meth.

A widely viewed basement video of Strings playing the song was filmed in a friend's basement while he and others were on mushrooms. The video is known for 'Barefoot Ben' in the background, and it had passed 29 million views by early 2024.
A live version recorded December 15, 2023 at Mohegan Sun Arena opens the 2024 album 'Live Vol. 1', which Billy Strings produced.

Billy Strings was born William Apostol in Lansing, MI, in 1992. He grew up in Michigan and Kentucky and was heavily influenced by his bluegrass-guitar-playing father. His 2019 album 'Home' won a Grammy.

research.lineage: The song is a fast, traditional-sounding bluegrass prison narrative by a player raised on Doc Watson, Bill Monroe and Larry Sparks, and it became a staple of his jamgrass-leaning live shows.

draft:
One phone call, and the narrator of **Dust in a Baggie** spends it on his father. Not a lawyer, not a friend from the crowd that got him here. "I used my only phone call to contact my daddy," Billy Strings sings, and the next line lands like a gavel: "I got 20 long years for some dust in a baggie." The phrasing does a lot of work. "Daddy" is a kid's word, reached for by a grown man who has nobody else. "Dust" makes the drug sound like almost nothing, which is the point. A lifetime traded for a speck in a plastic bag.

Strings has said he wrote it in about 30 minutes at work, with no guitar, just a melody in his head and a little notepad. He told Theo Von it's about Brad Lasco, the friend he later dedicated the *Me/And/Dad* record to, who had died a couple of years before. Strings has also described the song as being about a man who ruined his life and sits in prison wondering where he went wrong. Some traditional bluegrass fans waved it off as a song about meth. They missed the shame. The verses move from the binge (no sleep in seven days, the lighter under the bulb) to the regret of not listening to "mom and papa," and then to the line that strips the man down: "In here where they call me by a number, not a name." He isn't defiant and he isn't asking for pity. He's embarrassed, and he knows he's back "once again," so the regret comes with a suspicion it won't stick.

The band plays it fast and bright, which is how bluegrass has always handled a prison song. On this 2016 re-recording, the closing track of his self-titled EP, cut in Nashville at Minutia Studios, the banjo snaps out quick, percussive runs, and Casey Campbell's mandolin weaves fills around the vocal. Acoustic guitar keeps a hard rhythm and Erik Alvar's upright bass walks underneath. The room sounds clean and open. Strings sings in a clear, slightly raspy voice, conversational, more like someone telling you what happened than performing a lament. That plainness keeps the despair from going syrupy.

It's a player raised on Doc Watson, Bill Monroe and Larry Sparks writing a song that could pass for an old one, with a modern drug at the center. The song first appeared on *Rock of Ages*, his 2013 record with Don Julin. Later it became a live staple. A basement video, shot while Strings and friends were on mushrooms, passed 29 million views, and a 2023 Mohegan Sun performance opens *Live Vol. 1*.

The picking races ahead like nothing's wrong, and that's the trap: you're tapping your foot right up until you realize you're keeping time with a man counting out twenty years.
